summary: Describes the relationship between Internet Protocol addresses and addresses on several specific networks. It also shows the class A, B and C layout of the 32-bit internet address. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how Internet address fields correspond to addresses on several networks. It shows three address classes and the layouts used by early networks such as ARPANET.

subtitle: How early Internet address fields mapped to the local addresses of specific networks.

tldr.problem: Internet addresses include a network number and local address, while individual networks use different local address formats.
tldr.mechanism: The memo shows class A, B and C address layouts and maps local address fields for several networks into Internet addresses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 796 is Historic and replaces IEN 115. It records address mappings described in September 1981.

today: RFC 796 has Historic status and replaces IEN 115. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Internet Address Classes
sections.content:
An Internet address is a 32-bit quantity with a network number and a local address. The local address identifies a host within the network named by the network number.

Class A addresses use a 7-bit network number and a 24-bit local address. Class B uses a 14-bit network number and a 16-bit local address. Class C uses a 21-bit network number and an 8-bit local address.
sections.plainLanguage: An Internet address has a part for the network and a part for a host on that network. This memo describes three layouts for dividing those parts.

sections.title: Mapping Local Network Addresses
sections.content:
The memo shows how each network's own address fits into the local part of an Internet address. The ARPANET has network number 10 and uses its 24-bit host, logical-host and IMP fields directly; its logical-host field is set to zero because the IMPs did not yet support that addressing form.

Other examples include AUTODIN II (network 26), the Distributed Computing Networks at COMSAT and UCL (networks 29 and 30), the Experimental Data Network (21), LCSNET (18), several packet radio networks, SATNET (4) and WBCNET (28). The diagrams show which address bits each network uses.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network places its own address fields inside the local part of the Internet address. The memo gives separate layouts for the networks it describes.

sections.title: Different Local Address Fields
sections.content:
The address mappings vary with each network's address format. AUTODIN II and several packet radio networks use 16-bit host or subscriber addresses. The DCNs divide 16 bits into an 8-bit host identifier and an 8-bit process identifier.

SATNET addresses can be assigned independently of physical location, and a physical host may have several logical addresses. WBCNET divides its 16-bit address into a HAP number and a local address. These examples show why a network-specific mapping is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The network-specific fields can identify hosts, processes or logical addresses. The RFC explains each layout rather than defining one format for all networks.

sections.title: References and Scope
sections.content: This memo is a set of address mapping descriptions, not a procedure for assigning addresses. It refers to RFC 791 for the Internet Protocol specification and cites separate documents for additional WBCNET and LCSNET address details.
sections.plainLanguage: The document describes the mappings shown in its diagrams. It directs readers to other documents for additional details about some networks.

fields.name: Class bit
fields.desc: Leading zero marks a class A address.

references.text: Postel, J., "Internet Protocol - DARPA Internet Program Protocol Specification", RFC 791, September 1981.
